content: You are Truk8s Chat, an AI assistant for a Kubernetes dashboard. You help users understand and manage their Kubernetes cluster. You reply in English. You have real-time cluster data provided as context. Be concise and helpful. Use markdown for formatting.
What is Trustable?

Trustable is a Private AI workbench: a Lovable-like experience for building, running and publishing AI applications that never leave your own infrastructure. You describe what you want, Trustable writes it, and the result runs on your hardware — your models, your data, your cluster.
What does Trustable give you when it runs?

Trustable runs as a single local server that gives you three things at once: a workbench (the web UI where you list applications, edit their configuration and launch them), an AI coding assistant (the agent that turns a written description into a working frontend, backend actions and data wiring), and a complete runtime (Kubernetes, S3, PostgreSQL, Redis, object storage and serverless functions, already integrated, so a generated application has somewhere real to run).
How does Trustable store the source code of each application I create?

Each application you create lives in its own repository. Trustable keeps a durable copy of it and checks it out into a working area whenever you launch it, so you can edit, run, revert and publish without ever losing the source of truth.
What are the two states an application can be in inside Trustable?

Every application is in one or both of these states: Development — checked out and running locally, so you can iterate on it with the AI assistant and see changes immediately; and Production — published to your cluster, reachable by its own URL, serving real users. The workbench shows both at a glance, and you move an application from one to the other with a single action.
In what order should I read the Trustable documentation pages?

Read in order, the pages take you from a blank installation to a published application: 1) Setup — choosing the AI provider that powers the assistant; 2) Configuration — the workbench-wide settings: models, the coding model, your license, the template repository, shared environment values, Git and GitHub; 3) App List — the home screen, creating applications and every per-application action; 4) Editing — the workbench toolbar, the Config and Utils menus, committing, the device preview, redeploying; 5) Application chat — the AI assistant that writes your application, its agents, models and sessions; 6) Templates — reusable multi-step prompts.
What is the first thing I have to do when I open Trustable for the very first time?

The very first time you open Trustable you land on the splash screen, and before you can create an application Trustable needs to know which AI provider powers the assistant — the model that turns your descriptions into working code. This is the only mandatory setup step; everything else has a sensible default.
Which AI provider options does Trustable offer during setup?

The Select your AI provider screen offers three cards, and the difference between them is where the model runs and who pays for it: Cloud AI — subscription-based AI powered by Ollama Cloud, where Trustable talks to its own built-in Ollama server which forwards to Ollama's cloud models (you need a free Ollama Cloud account); Sovereign AI — credit-based AI powered by Regolo.AI with models hosted in the EU (you need a Trustable AI account, which comes with 100 free credits on sign-up); and Private AI — any OpenAI-compatible endpoint you run yourself, where nothing leaves your infrastructure (you need the URL of your own endpoint).
Do I have to choose the AI provider every time I start Trustable?
No. Whichever provider you pick, the choice is saved in your workspace configuration and Trustable goes straight to the application list next time. You can change it later from the Configure page.
What happens right after I select an AI provider in Trustable?

Trustable runs a short configuration pass: it pulls the models it needs (for Cloud AI), writes the runtime configuration for the Pi coding agent, and finishes with a live "Reply with exactly: OK" probe against the model. Only when that probe succeeds are you let through to the application list — an unusable model would make the whole workbench useless, so a failed check always sends you back to the provider screen.
Why is Cloud AI described as the fastest way to start with Trustable?

Cloud AI uses the Ollama server bundled inside Trustable, and that server forwards your requests to Ollama Cloud's large models, so you get cloud-class quality without installing anything or managing a GPU. Signing up for Ollama Cloud is free and includes a free allowance you can upgrade later, and there is nothing to type into Trustable — no URL and no API key. Instead you pair the machine with your Ollama account once.
Why does the first Cloud AI configuration attempt fail, and what should I do?

The first configuration attempt is expected to fail if you have never paired the device. Trustable detects the authentication failure and shows a "Sign-in required" message: it has run `ollama signin` in the background and scraped the pairing URL out of it. Click "Click here to log in to Ollama Cloud" — it opens in a new tab, so the Trustable page stays where it is.
What if Trustable cannot find the Ollama pairing URL?
If Trustable cannot find a pairing URL, it shows a different message asking you to run `ollama signin` yourself in a terminal and then click Retry.
What are the two names shown on the Ollama device-pairing page?

The Ollama page asks you to confirm your account and pair that specific machine. The two names shown are the host and the cluster Trustable is running on, so you can tell one installation from another. You then click Connect.
Do I have to pair my device with Ollama Cloud every time?
No. After "Device Connected Successfully", the identity is stored in the Trustable workspace, so it survives restarts — you only do this once per installation. You can then close the Ollama tab.
What progress messages does Trustable show when the Cloud AI configuration pass reruns after Retry?

The configuration pass reruns, now authenticated, and streams its progress: `Pulling model …` / `OK: … pulled` — one line per model in the recommended Cloud AI set being fetched into the local Ollama server; `OK: Pi global configuration written` — the coding agent now knows which provider, endpoint and models to use; and `Testing AI model connection…` followed by `OK: AI model connection successful` — the live probe passed. Clicking CONTINUE takes you to the application list.
How is Sovereign AI billed and how many free credits do I get?

Sovereign AI routes your requests through Regolo.AI, an EU-hosted inference provider, and bills them as credits rather than as a subscription. Registering gives you 100 credits free, which is enough to build and iterate on a first application.
Do I have to copy and paste an API key when I use Sovereign AI?

No. Choosing the Sovereign AI card opens the Trustable AI registration page inside Trustable as an overlay, and when you finish that page hands the endpoint and API key straight back to Trustable — you never copy and paste a key.
What information does the Trustable AI account registration form ask for?

The Create account form asks for your name, email, phone (with country code), a password of at least 8 characters, and optionally your company and LinkedIn. You must accept the Privacy Policy and pass the human-verification check, then click Send verification code and confirm the code sent to you.
Why does the password of my Trustable AI account matter after sign-up?

The password matters beyond sign-up because it is what you use later to sign in again and recover your API key. The sign-in page also carries Forgot password? and Top up your account links; topping up is reachable later from inside the workbench when your credits run low.
Does Sovereign AI need to pull any models during the configuration pass?

No. For Sovereign AI there are no models to pull — the models are remote — so only the "Reply with exactly: OK" probe runs, and it is quick. When registration completes, the overlay closes on its own and Trustable saves the returned endpoint and key.
What happens if my Sovereign AI key later expires or runs out of credits?
If the probe ever fails later — an expired or exhausted key, for instance — Trustable reopens the same Trustable AI registration overlay so you can sign in again, then retries automatically.
What kind of endpoints can I use with the Private AI option?

Private AI is the option for your own hardware: an Ollama server on your network, a vLLM deployment, a llama.cpp server, or any other service that speaks the OpenAI-compatible API. Nothing about your prompts or code leaves the machines you control, and there is no per-token cost.
What does the Private AI dialog ask for, and what format must the URL have?

The dialog asks for two things: Base URL — required, it must end in `/v1` (the OpenAI-compatible API root) and match the shape `http(s)://…/v1`; Trustable refuses to save anything else, because a wrong URL would otherwise fail much later in a confusing place. And API key — optional, since many self-hosted endpoints need none, which is exactly the case this card is named for.
What is a typical Private AI endpoint entry?
A typical entry is a plain `http://` address on your LAN, like an Ollama server listening on port `11434`. Because it is `http://` and unauthenticated, it saves with no further questions.
Why does Trustable ask me to confirm when I enter an https Private AI URL with no API key?

If you enter an `https://` URL and leave the API key empty, Trustable asks you to confirm — a public HTTPS endpoint almost always requires a key, so an empty one is usually a mistake rather than a choice.
What does Trustable do when I press SAVE on a Private AI endpoint?

Trustable immediately queries the endpoint for its model list rather than trusting the URL blindly. On success it reports how many models it found and tells you the one remaining step. A broken endpoint, or one that returns no models at all, is reported right in the dialog and is never saved.
Why doesn't Trustable pick the coding model automatically for a Private AI endpoint?

Unlike Cloud AI and Sovereign AI, a private endpoint carries no catalog telling Trustable which of its models is good at writing code. Picking one automatically would silently select an embedding or a tiny model and fail confusingly later, so Trustable deliberately makes no guess and asks you, taking you to the Configure page with the banner "Choose the Pi model to complete the runtime setup."
What does the Configure page show after a Private AI endpoint is discovered?

It shows three things: Private AI Endpoint — the URL in use (to point at a different endpoint, use Change Provider and pick Private AI again); Private AI Models — every model discovered at the endpoint with its context size and a FOR CODING verdict, marked either `Available` or `Hidden` with the reason, typically "below the recommended 20B minimum", with ADD MODEL to declare a model the endpoint did not advertise and REMOVE to drop one; and Pi Model → Default Model — the dropdown where you pick the model the coding assistant will use, offering only `Available` models. Clicking SAVE & CONFIGURE writes the configuration and runs the "Reply with exactly: OK" probe.
Why are small models hidden from the coding-model choice?

Models below the recommended 20B parameter minimum are marked `Hidden` with that reason, since small models cannot reliably drive the coding agent. Embedding, rerank and vision models are hidden for the same purpose.
Why is SAVE & CONFIGURE blocked and what message do I get?
The button is blocked while no default model is selected, and Trustable tells you "Please select the default model before saving."
How do I reach the Configure page in Trustable, and what does it cover?

The Configure page is reached from the Configure button on the App List. It is where you review and change everything that applies to the whole workbench rather than to a single application: which AI provider is in use, which models are available and which one writes your code, your license, your Git identity, and the values shared across applications.
How is the Configure page laid out and which button saves it?

The page is a stack of cards rendered top to bottom. One button at the very bottom — Save & Configure — commits the model-related cards. A few cards (Predefined Environment Variables, License, GitHub Account) save themselves independently so that editing them does not re-run a model test.
Can I change my AI provider after setup, and why isn't it re-prompted?

Yes: next to the header stating which provider is active there is a Change Provider button that takes you back to the provider-choice screen, and picking a provider there reseeds the model list from scratch. Provider choice is deliberately not re-prompted on the Configure page — once you have a provider, Configure always opens straight into the model editor.
What does the Ollama Host card do?

When the provider is Ollama, the Ollama Host card appears directly under the header. Using the internal Ollama server — the normal Cloud AI case — there is nothing to set, and the card says so: "Using internal Ollama — click Change Provider if you want to use your own." Pointing Trustable at an Ollama server of your own is done through the Private AI card on the provider screen, which asks for the endpoint URL and then discovers its models directly from your machine.
What columns does the provider models table have on the Configure page?

Each row carries: MODEL — the model identifier exactly as the provider names it, where the `:cloud` suffix marks Ollama Cloud models that run remotely rather than on your machine; CONTEXT SIZE — editable, how much text the model can consider at once in tokens, where leaving it empty means use the default (128 000); MAX OUTPUT — editable, the upper bound on a single reply, default 32K; FOR CODING — whether the model can be selected to drive the coding agent; and ACTIONS — REMOVE deletes the row, and ADD MODEL at the top adds one. The heading follows the provider, so it reads Ollama Models, Trustable Models or Private AI Models.
What is the default context size and default max output for a model in Trustable?
Leaving CONTEXT SIZE empty means "use the default", which is 128 000 tokens. The default MAX OUTPUT — the upper bound on a single reply — is 32K.
What does the FOR CODING column mean, and why are hidden models still listed?

FOR CODING says whether the model can be selected to drive the coding agent. `Available` means yes. `Hidden`, with a short reason, means no — typically an embedding, rerank or vision model, or one below the recommended 20B parameter minimum. Hidden models stay visible in the table on purpose, so you can see what your provider actually offers, but they cannot be chosen as the coding model.
Does adding or removing a model in the table change the provider's catalog?
No. ADD MODEL and REMOVE edit your list only, never the provider's catalog: use them to hide models you never want to see, or to declare one your endpoint did not advertise.
Which provider model lists can I edit and which are read-only?
Ollama and Private AI lists are yours to edit. The Sovereign AI (Trustable) list is authoritative and read-only; instead of Add/Remove it offers a Refresh button that re-fetches the catalog.
What happens when my provider publishes a new model catalog version?

Trustable notices on the next page load, saves the new list, and sends you back to the Configure page with a banner asking you to re-pick the coding model — because the one you had chosen may no longer exist.
What is Pi in Trustable and what is the Default Model setting?

Pi is the coding agent inside Trustable — the thing that reads your request and writes the code. The Default Model dropdown on the Pi Model card is where you choose which model it uses, and it is the single most consequential setting on the Configure page. The dropdown lists only models marked `Available` in the table above, so you cannot accidentally point the agent at an embedding model, and the rule is enforced on the server too, not just in the browser. A checkmark marks the current selection, and there is no separate "small" or "secondary" model to configure — one choice covers all agent work.
What does a Trustable license enable, and what works without one?

A license enables Git push and publishing to production. Everything else — creating applications, editing them with the AI assistant, running them locally, committing to the local repository — works without one. The License card only appears when licensing is enabled on your installation.
How do I install a Trustable license and how do I obtain one?

Paste the token you were issued — it starts with `lic_` — into the License box and click SAVE LICENSE. To obtain one, write to info@nuvolaris.io or visit nuvolaris.io. The status line tells you where you stand, for example "No license installed. Git push and publishing are disabled."
Is Trustable license verification done online?
No, verification is completely offline: the license is a signed statement checked against a public key built into Trustable, so no network call and no license server is involved.
What does a Trustable license encode?

It encodes: who it was issued to and when; an optional expiry date — the license is valid through the whole of that day and invalid from the next one, and an expired license disables Git push as well as publishing; and the list of cluster hosts you may publish to — publishing to a host not on that list is refused even with a perfectly valid license, though local development clusters are exempt from the host check while still requiring a valid license.
How do I configure where prompt templates come from?

The Template Repository card on the Configure page configures the source used by every application. It has: Repository — the `owner/name` of the GitHub repository holding the templates, default `trustable-ai/templates`; Branch / ref — which branch or tag to read, default `main`; and GitHub token — needed only to write.
Do I need a GitHub token to use templates?
Only to write. Reading public templates works without one, but saving, adding and removing templates from inside an application stays disabled until a token is configured, as the card warns.
How is the GitHub token for templates stored and how do I remove it?

The token field is write-only: Trustable shows whether a token exists but never displays it back. Leaving the field blank keeps the one already stored; to get rid of it, tick "Remove the configured token". The token is stored as a protected file in your workspace, never in the shared configuration file, and is used only by Trustable itself.
Can a single application use a different template repository from the workbench default?
Yes. An individual application can override the repository — a starter can bring its own template set — while the Template Repository card supplies the default for everything else.
What are Predefined Environment Variables in Trustable?

Applications declare the environment variables they need — an API key, a database URL — and values shared across several applications would otherwise have to be retyped for each one. The Predefined Environment Variables card is where you keep them once. It is a palette, not a source: "Nothing is applied automatically — you confirm them in the application's own environment editor." A predefined value never silently reaches an application; when a newly created or imported application asks for a variable it has no value for, its environment editor offers a Use predefined values button, and only then, and only after you save there, does the value land in that application.
What controls does the Predefined Environment Variables card offer?

ADD VARIABLE — appends an empty row for you to fill in; names must look like shell variables: letters, digits and underscores, not starting with a digit. IMPORT FROM FILE — fills the table from a local `.env`-style file, parsed in your browser and never uploaded; values from the file win over rows already in the table, and if any name is invalid the whole import is refused rather than half-applied. SAVE VARIABLES — persists the table; this card saves on its own, does not run a model test and does not navigate away.
What happens to a predefined environment variable whose value I leave empty?
An empty value is kept rather than dropped: it records the name as something you intend to fill in, and it will not satisfy an application's requirement in the meantime.
What is the Git User card and why does it sometimes disappear?

The Git User card holds the name and email stamped on commits Trustable makes on your behalf — when you press Commit in the editor, or when it auto-commits a generated file. The card is visible while no GitHub account is connected; connecting one hides it, because the connected account already supplies the identity and showing both would be misleading. Your values are not deleted — disconnecting GitHub brings the card back with them intact.
How do I connect a GitHub account to Trustable?

On the GitHub Account card, click CONNECT GITHUB to start the GitHub device login: Trustable shows a one-time code and a button to open GitHub, you approve there, and the card switches to connected with your login name. A Disconnect action removes the connection and every credential Trustable stored for it. The pill on the right shows the current state, for example DISCONNECTED. You connect one personal `github.com` account so Trustable can import and push public or private repositories on your behalf.
Are my GitHub credentials exposed to the AI assistant or to my applications?

No. Credentials are held in an isolated, protected area of your workspace. They are never handed to the AI assistant, to your applications' environment files, or to any terminal you open in the workbench.
Is a connected GitHub account preferred over an SSH key in Trustable?

Yes. A connected account is the preferred way to reach repositories, over HTTPS. An SSH key remains available as a fallback and is offered behind a collapsed "Use an SSH key instead" option where a repository is needed. The same connect form appears wherever a repository is needed — the Git Push popup, the Add Application dialog — and it is the same connection everywhere.
Does connecting GitHub give me the right to publish in Trustable?
No. GitHub authentication is entirely separate from publishing authorization. Connecting GitHub does not grant the right to publish; that is the license.
What exactly does the SAVE & CONFIGURE button do on the Configure page?

SAVE & CONFIGURE commits the provider, model table and Pi model settings, then immediately verifies them: it saves, then asks the chosen model to reply `OK`. The button reports progress inline — "Saving configuration…", "Testing connection…", "Success" — and on success returns you to the application list. The License, Predefined Environment Variables and GitHub Account cards have their own actions and are not covered by this button.
What happens if the connection test after SAVE & CONFIGURE fails?

You stay on the Configure page with the error shown in a red box and a Retry button. Nothing bounces you back to the splash screen, because that would only re-run the same broken settings; instead you correct the form and try again.
What is the application list in Trustable?

The application list is Trustable's home screen. Everything you build lives there, and every action that operates on a whole application — open it, edit its environment, sync it with GitHub, publish it, remove it — starts from that page.
What are the four bands of the Trustable application list page?

The header (Trustable logo, product name, a compact release tag such as `V0.4.0 · MAIN`, and the global CONFIGURE and ADD APP buttons); the summary row (four counts); the Applications card labelled WORKBENCH INVENTORY, which is the list itself with its search box, sort selector, view switch and filters; and the footer, which reports the build identifier and the expiry date of this Trustable version plus a short hash identifying the ops task set in use.
What does hovering the release tag in the Trustable header reveal?
Hovering the release tag reveals the exact source branch and build label, which is how you tell a local build from a development or release image.
What do the four counters in the summary row of the app list mean?

APPLICATIONS — how many you have in total; PRODUCTION — how many are configured for production, i.e. have a cluster to publish to; DEVELOPMENT — how many exist only locally so far; and REPOSITORIES — how many have a Git repository behind them.
Do Trustable builds expire?
Yes. The footer reports the build identifier and the expiry date of the Trustable version you are running; past it, the app asks you to update.
When does the Credits pill appear on the application list?

When your provider is Sovereign AI, a Credits pill appears just under the title showing your remaining balance, refreshed every minute. With any other provider there are no credits to track and the pill is not shown.
What are the two ways to create a new application in Trustable?

ADD APP opens the Add Application dialog, which presents two ways as tabs: start from a Starter — an empty but correctly wired skeleton you then describe to the AI — or pick a ready-made application from the catalog and adapt it.
Which starters does Trustable offer?

The STARTER tab is the default and offers a short radio list of minimal, convention-compatible repositories maintained for Trustable, each with its name linking to its GitHub page and a one-line description: truchat — AI chat UI with RAG; trudemo — collection of demos; trureact — a generic React starter; and My Application Starter, always the last row, for using a repository of your own rather than a published starter.
What are the naming rules for a new Trustable application?

The Application Name must be 6–20 alphanumeric characters starting with a letter, and it must not collide with an application you already have. It is the identity the application keeps everywhere: its repository, its workspace, its URL.
What is the GitHub Repository field in the Add Application dialog?

It is the repository in `org/repo` form where the code comes from. It is prefilled from the starter you selected; choosing My Application Starter is what makes this field yours to fill in. That is also the case where a private repository may need a connected GitHub account, so the dialog offers to connect one there.
What happens when I press CREATE in the Add Application dialog?

Trustable clones the starter into a durable repository of its own for this app, registers it, and returns you to the list. If the starter declares environment variables with no value, Trustable asks you to fill them in before going further.
How does Trustable discover the list of starters?

Starters are discovered from a published index rather than by querying GitHub, so the list is identical on every installation. If it cannot be loaded, the dialog says so and leaves My Application Starter available, so you are never stuck.
What are the catalog tabs in the Add Application dialog and how do they work?

The tabs CHAT, DEMO, EXAMPLES and UTILITIES browse the catalog of complete, working applications. Each tab is one group shown as a carousel: one application at a time, with its title at the top linking to its GitHub repository, a screenshot in the middle, and its description underneath. The ‹ and › arrows step through the group and wrap around at both ends, and the arrow keys do the same; a "1 of 3" counter tells you how far along you are. A group holding a single application shows neither arrows nor counter.
What kinds of applications are in the CHAT, DEMO, EXAMPLES and UTILITIES catalog groups?

CHAT collects conversational applications — for example AI Database Manager, an interface that turns plain-language questions into live PostgreSQL work. DEMO holds showcase applications demonstrating what Trustable can build — for example AI CRM, a contact-and-ticket dashboard. EXAMPLES holds worked examples you can learn from or build on — for example API Status Monitor, which polls endpoints and records uptime, response times and check history. UTILITIES holds practical tools — for example Document Ingest, which uploads PDFs and runs them through an ingestion pipeline so an AI application can search them.
What happens when I click a catalog application card in Trustable?

Clicking anywhere on the card except the title link opens a small name panel: it names the application and the repository it will be created from, prefills an Application Name, and offers Cancel and Confirm. The prefilled name is only a starting point — you can edit it freely, and if the obvious name is taken Trustable appends the smallest free number (`tetris`, `tetris1`, `tetris2`). Cancel returns to the carousel rather than closing the dialog, because you are choosing, not aborting.
Can the same application appear in more than one catalog group?

Yes. An application can be listed under more than one group. Whichever tab you create it from, it is created from that entry's own repository, so two entries in the same group give you two genuinely different applications.
Does switching tabs in the Add Application dialog lose what I typed?
No. Switching tabs never loses what you typed elsewhere: the Starter tab keeps its selection and name. Reopening the dialog always resets to Starter.
What does the APPLICATION column show in the Trustable app list?

It identifies each application with a colour-coded initials badge, the application name, and — when it is running — a DEVELOPMENT link that opens the live local application in a new tab. That link is how you look at what you are building outside the editor.
What filters can I apply to the Trustable application list?

Three segmented filters restrict what the list shows and combine with the search box, with the "N applications" count following both: ALL — the default, every application whatever its state; PRODUCTION — only applications configured for production, meaning they have a cluster host, user and credentials recorded and can be published; and DEVELOPMENT ONLY — the complement, applications that exist only locally and have never been given a production target, useful for spotting work that is ready to ship but not yet configured.
How does search work on the Trustable application list?

The Search apps or repositories box filters as you type, entirely in the browser with no round trip to the server. It matches the application name, the repository, and the production host and user, so you can find an application by where it is deployed as well as by what it is called. Next to it, Name is the sort selector — sort by application name or by repository — and GRID / LIST is the view switch, with LIST as the default dense table.
What is the difference between the Grid and List views in Trustable?

GRID shows each application as a card instead of a table row, carrying the same information laid out vertically: the initials badge and name, the repository link, state chips (Development, REPO), then two wide buttons for the environments — DEVELOPMENT, which opens the running local application, and NO PRODUCTION, which is inert and simply reports that this application has no published deployment yet — with the actions at the bottom of the card. Grid is the better view when applications have screenshots or you are scanning a handful of them; List is better once you have many.
What does the REPOSITORY column show and how does it differ from Trustable's own copy?

The REPOSITORY column shows the GitHub repository backing the application, as `org/repo`, linked to its GitHub page. This is the code's public home — the target of Git Pull and Git Push — as distinct from the durable local copy Trustable keeps for itself.
What does the STATUS column of the application list report?
It reports which of the two states the application is in: DEVELOPMENT when it exists only locally, and PRODUCTION once it has been published to a cluster and is serving real users.
What actually happens when I press EDIT on an application?

EDIT opens the application in the workbench editor, where you talk to the AI assistant and watch your application update live. Clicking it launches the application, which is real work: Trustable checks the code out into a working area, regenerates its configuration files, logs in to the cluster, installs dependencies and starts the development server. A progress bar tracks the actual lifecycle stages rather than a timer, so it reflects genuine progress; if a stage fails, the bar stops where it got to and the error is shown.
Is it safe to click EDIT twice on the same Trustable application?
Yes. Clicking Edit again — from the same tab or another — is safe. Trustable reuses a runtime that is already healthy instead of starting a second one.
What does the ENV button on an application row open?

ENV opens the environment editor for that application: a table with a VARIABLE column and separate Development and Production values, so one application can point at a test database locally and the real one in production.
Which environment variables are fixed and cannot be removed in a Trustable application?

Four rows are fixed: OPS_APIHOST — the cluster the application publishes to; OPS_USER and OPS_PASSWORD — its credentials on that cluster; and OPS_REPO — its production repository, initialized from the Git origin. For these, the development value is managed by Trustable and read-only, while the production value is yours to set. Below them you add and remove your own variables freely.
How do I import environment values from a file in the application environment editor?

Import `.env` and Import `.env.production` fill a column from a local file, parsed in the browser. Neither import writes anything until you press Save, which writes both files; Close warns you if changes are pending. Values kept in Predefined Environment Variables are also offered here through a Use predefined values button when a required variable has no value, and nothing is copied in without you confirming it.
What does GIT PULL do in Trustable and where does it pull from?

GIT PULL brings changes from GitHub into Trustable — work done elsewhere, by a teammate or by you on another machine. It pulls from the configured production repository when there is one, and from the application's original origin otherwise, then updates both Trustable's durable copy and, if the application is checked out, the working copy.
Can Git Pull in Trustable overwrite my uncommitted work?

No. The pull is deliberately conservative: it never merges, rebases, hard-resets or overwrites uncommitted work. If you have local changes or the histories have diverged, it stops and tells you, leaving your work untouched — commit or set your changes aside first, then pull again.
Does Trustable redeploy automatically after a Git Pull?
No. When the pull did change the checked-out copy, Trustable asks whether you want to deploy as well, since fresh code usually needs redeploying to take effect. Declining changes nothing.
What does GIT PUSH ask for the first time, and how does it authenticate?

The first push for an application needs a target, so Trustable asks for the production repository in `org/repo` form. The same dialog offers to connect your GitHub account, which is the recommended path: Trustable then pushes over HTTPS using the connection, with no key to manage. If you would rather not connect an account, a collapsed "Use an SSH deploy key instead" option reveals a key you can add to the repository's deploy keys with write access. Once configured, the repository is remembered and later pushes go straight through.
Which branch does Trustable push to?
Trustable pushes the repository's own default branch rather than assuming `main`.
Does Git Push require a license in Trustable?
Yes. Git Push requires a valid license. Without one, Trustable offers to install a license rather than failing silently.
What does PUBLISH do and what does it ask for the first time?

PUBLISH deploys the application to your OpenServerless cluster and moves it into the Production state, reachable at its own URL by real users. The first publish asks for the cluster details — OPS_APIHOST, OPS_USER and OPS_PASSWORD — since Trustable cannot guess where you want it to run; the dialog notes that you need an OpenServerless environment and points at info@nuvolaris.io or the OpenServerless project if you do not have one. With the target known, Trustable prepares a clean checkout, generates the production environment files, logs in to the cluster in production mode, and deploys. Later publishes skip straight to the deployment.
What are the license requirements for publishing an application?

Publish requires a valid license, and the license must cover the specific cluster host you are publishing to — a valid license for one cluster does not authorize another. Local development clusters are exempt from the host check but still need a valid license.
What does UNDEPLOY do, and does it need a license?

UNDEPLOY is the counterpart of Publish: it removes the application's deployed actions and packages from the cluster, taking it out of production. It is deliberately narrow — your code, your local repository, your configuration and the application's entry in the list are all untouched, only the running deployment goes away, and you can publish again at any time. Because of that narrowness it needs no license. A confirmation modal asks "Undeploy <name>? This removes its deployed actions and packages." before anything happens, and the command output is shown when it finishes.
Why does Undeploy say "workbench not found — launch the app first"?

Undeploy runs inside the application's checked-out copy using cluster credentials, so an application that has never been opened has nothing to undeploy from, and Trustable replies "workbench not found — launch the app first."
What exactly does DELETE remove in Trustable?

DELETE removes the application from Trustable — its entry, its local repository and its checkout. It is styled in red because it is the only genuinely destructive action on the page and, unlike Undeploy, it does not leave the source behind. Anything you have pushed to GitHub survives, since Delete acts on Trustable's copy rather than on the remote repository; anything you have not pushed is gone. If the work matters, Git Push before you delete.
What is the layout of the Trustable workbench that EDIT opens?

The workbench is a toolbar over two panes. The left pane is the AI assistant, TruACP — a full conversation with the coding agent, with a message box at the bottom that also runs shell commands when you prefix them with `!`. The right pane is your application running live — the real thing, not a mockup — which updates when the assistant changes code and which you can click through exactly as your users will. The divider between them can be dragged to give either side more room.
How do the two halves of the workbench toolbar differ?

The toolbar splits in two: controls on the left act on the assistant and the application's configuration, and controls on the right act on the preview and your changes. On the left, from left to right: the sidebar toggle, then the TUTORIAL, TERMINAL, CONFIG and UTILS buttons. On the right: the git status pill, COMMIT, the three device buttons, ROUTE, RELOAD and BACK.
What does the hide-chat button do, and does hiding stop the assistant?

The panel icon hides and shows the assistant pane so the preview can take the full width — useful when you want to look at your application properly rather than at the conversation. As the in-app tutorial puts it: "This button hides and shows the assistant pane on the left. Hiding it gives the preview the full width; your session keeps running either way." The assistant is only hidden visually, never stopped — nothing is reloaded and no conversation is lost, so you can toggle it as often as you like, and the choice is remembered between sessions.
Which guided tutorials does the workbench offer?

The TUTORIAL pulldown starts guided walkthroughs that spotlight each control in place and explain it. There are three: TEMPLATES — the prompt templates in the assistant pane; MENUS — the Config and Utils pulldowns; and TOOLBAR — the right-hand group: Commit, the device preview, Route, Reload and Back. The Templates tutorial needs the assistant pane visible, so if you have hidden it the tutorial highlights the toggle first and waits for you to bring it back.
What is the TERMINAL button in the Trustable workbench?

TERMINAL opens a real shell inside your application's directory, in a pane below the two panes rather than replacing either of them. It is a genuine terminal, not a command box: interactive programs, editors and long-running processes all work. Drag its top edge to resize it and the height is remembered; closing the pane ends the shell, so its visibility is deliberately not restored on the next visit.
What is in the CONFIG menu of the workbench?

CONFIG holds the settings of the application you are editing — as the tutorial says, "its environment variables, the skills the assistant can use, and its AGENTS.md." It has three entries: Env, Skills and AGENTS.md.
What does the Env entry in the workbench Config menu do?

It opens the environment-variable editor with separate development and production values, exactly like the ENV button on the app list. It is also where the launch process sends you when an application is missing a required value, so a blocked launch can be fixed without leaving the workbench.
What are Skills in Trustable?

Skills are ready-made abilities you add to the assistant for a particular application — packaged instructions that teach it a particular job. Adding one clones it into the application so the assistant picks it up.
What is AGENTS.md and why should I use it?

`AGENTS.md` is the instructions file the assistant reads before doing anything in your application. It is where you record what the assistant cannot infer from the code: conventions to follow, libraries to prefer, things never to touch. Time spent there pays for itself — it is the difference between explaining your project in every message and explaining it once. The entry opens an editor with Save and Cancel, and the file is created and added to Git if it does not exist yet.
What actions are in the UTILS menu of the Trustable workbench?
UTILS holds the actions you run against the application itself — "from reloading it to inspecting its files." It has seven entries, in order: Revert, Reload, Redeploy, Clean, Debug, Files and Upload.
What does REVERT do in the workbench, and when is it disabled?

REVERT discards every uncommitted change and returns the application to its last commit. It is greyed out when there is nothing to revert — the same condition that disables Commit. It asks for confirmation, and it means what it asks: reverting removes untracked new files as well as edits, so anything not committed is gone.
What is the difference between RELOAD and REDEPLOY in Trustable?

RELOAD refreshes the preview pane only — nothing runs on the server. It is the cheap refresh for the usual case, where the dev server has already rebuilt in the background. REDEPLOY rebuilds on the server first, which is what you need after changing dependencies or configuration, since those are not picked up by a browser refresh; it runs a full cycle (stop the dev server, deploy the backend actions, list them, start the dev server, wait for it to answer) and reports each step in the preview pane as it goes.
Why is Redeploy in the Utils menu when it is also on the toolbar?
Redeploy is in the Utils menu on purpose: the toolbar reaches it only through a modifier key, so the menu is the discoverable path to it.
What does CLEAN do, and what does it not do?

CLEAN removes the application's local build artefacts — the virtual environment, `node_modules`, built archives — and nothing else. It does not rebuild. Cleaning stops the dev server, so the preview goes down and stays down until you redeploy; a plain Reload cannot bring it back, which is why the result panel offers a Redeploy button directly. Use it when a build has got into a state you no longer trust and you want to start from clean dependencies.
Where do I look when something in my application does not work and the preview gives no clue?

Use DEBUG, which opens a separate window streaming the live log of your running application — where build errors, runtime exceptions and the output of your backend actions actually appear. The log streams as it happens, and closing the window stops it.
What can I do with the FILES entry in the workbench Utils menu?

FILES browses the application's source read-only: a file tree on the left, content on the right, with a Copy button and a Refresh for the tree. It is for reading what the assistant has written — reviewing a change, checking where something lives — without leaving Trustable. There is deliberately no edit, create, rename or delete: editing happens through the assistant or the terminal. Content is always shown as plain text, so markdown appears as its source rather than rendered.
How do I give the assistant a file such as an image, a PDF or a dataset?

Use UPLOAD, which puts a file into your application so the assistant can work with it. After the upload Trustable shows the full path and lets you copy it, which is what you paste into your next message to point the assistant at the file.
What does the git status pill in the workbench show?

The status pill polls the application every ten seconds and reports it: NO CHANGES with a green dot when everything is saved, or an orange dot with a summary like "3 changed, 1 added, 2 deleted" when it is not.
Why is committing important in Trustable and not just optional housekeeping?

COMMIT saves the current state of the application into its durable repository, and is disabled while there is nothing to save. The working copy the assistant edits is temporary — it does not survive a restart of the application, and uncommitted work is permanently lost when that happens. Committing is the only way to keep it, so commit whenever the application reaches a state you would be unhappy to lose.
What device viewports does the Trustable preview offer, and at what sizes?

Three segmented buttons — desktop, tablet, phone — constrain the preview to a device viewport: tablet at 820×1180 and phone at 390×844, while desktop fills the pane with no frame. Your choice is remembered between sessions.
Does scaling the device preview affect how my application's responsive rules behave?

No. The device frames scale down to fit the pane, but the scaling is visual only: the preview still reports the true device width to your application, so its own responsive rules fire exactly as they would on the real hardware. That is the whole point — a shrunken desktop layout would tell you nothing.
What is the ROUTE button and the Route & Query dialog?

The ROUTE button shows which page the preview is on — `ROUTE: /` for the home page — and clicking it opens the Route & Query dialog. Route is the path the preview opens at: set it to `/settings` to work on that page directly instead of clicking your way there after every reload. Query Parameters are key/value pairs appended as a query string; "+ Add parameter" adds a row, each row has a × to remove it, and rows with an empty key are ignored. OK applies both and reloads the preview at the new address; CANCEL leaves everything untouched. Your choice persists, so reloads keep landing on the page you are working on.
What does the toolbar RELOAD button do exactly?
RELOAD refreshes the preview, keeping the current route and query and busting the cache. There is no server call and no waiting.
How do I trigger a redeploy from the toolbar instead of the Utils menu?

Hold Shift and the RELOAD button becomes REDEPLOY — rocket icon and all — running the full server-side rebuild. The label changes while you hold the key, before you click, so the modifier is visible rather than hidden. Both actions are also in the Utils menu if you would rather not use the modifier.
What happens when I press BACK in the workbench with uncommitted changes?

BACK leaves the workbench and returns to the application list, stopping the application's processes on the way out. If you have uncommitted changes it warns you first, under the heading "Uncommitted Changes", offering Go back anyway and Cancel. Leaving is not itself destructive — it only stops the running processes — but the working copy does not survive a restart, so uncommitted work will be lost the next time the application is launched. The warning is about that risk, not about the navigation; if in doubt, Cancel and Commit first.
What is TruACP?

TruACP is the Trustable Agent Control Panel — the left pane of the workbench, and a full coding agent rather than a chat widget. It has three parts: a toolbar along the top, the conversation in the middle, and the message box at the bottom. You describe what you want in ordinary language and the assistant writes the code, creates the backend actions, wires the data, and the preview on the right updates.
What does the assistant's opening message report, and why does the MCP line matter?

The opening message reports what is running: `pi v0.82.0`, the agent's loaded extensions, and — the important line — "MCP: 8 servers connected (126 tools)". Those tools are the assistant's hands. Through them it reaches your PostgreSQL database, Redis, object storage, the vector database and the serverless runtime directly, which is why it can build a working application rather than only produce files.
What is on the TruACP toolbar?
The toolbar, left to right: the agent selector, a connection indicator, the model selector, then new session, resume session, templates, run next step and run all steps.
Which coding agents can Trustable drive?

The agent selector dropdown chooses between Claude Code, Codex and Pi. Pi is the default and the one Trustable configures for you — the model you picked during setup is Pi's model. The dot next to the selector shows the connection state of the selected agent.
Does changing the model in the TruACP toolbar change my default model?

No. The model selector sets the model the agent uses for this session — for example `ollama/Glm 5.2 Cloud`. It is prefilled from your configured default, and changing it there affects this session only; the permanent default lives on the Configuration page. Switching model mid-project is a normal thing to do: a larger model for architectural work, a faster one for small mechanical edits.
When should I start a new session with the assistant?

The + button starts a fresh conversation, clearing the context the assistant is carrying. Start a new session when you move to an unrelated task: a long conversation about the login page is dead weight — and cost — when you turn to the reporting screen, and a clean start usually produces better results than one crowded with irrelevant history. Your code is untouched; only the conversation resets.
How do I go back to an earlier assistant conversation?

The clock icon — resume session — reopens an earlier session with its context intact, which is useful when you come back to work you left half-finished, or after a new session turns out to have been premature. Sessions belong to the application and survive leaving the workbench, so yesterday's conversation is still there tomorrow.
What is a template in Trustable?

A template is an ordered list of prompts — a recipe. Instead of typing five instructions in sequence and waiting for each, you load a template and run its steps, in order, one at a time or all at once. Templates are the answer to work you do repeatedly: adding a page, adding an API endpoint, wiring a database table. Someone writes the sequence once, and everyone runs it.
What are the three parts of the Templates panel?

Source — the GitHub repository and branch the catalog is read from, for example `trustable-ai/templates · main`, with a Refresh button; it is set on the Configuration page. The working copy — at the top in its own box, the template currently loaded into your application, shown with its name (for example App Suite), where it came from, and an Open button. The catalog — the templates available in the source repository, each with its name and description, such as Add API (add an API endpoint), Add Database and Add Page (add a React page); selecting one copies it into your application as the new working copy.
Where does the loaded template live inside my application?
The working copy lives in your application as `template.md`, so a template travels with the application and is published with it.
Why does the Templates panel say to add a GitHub token in configuration?

The note "add in configuration your github token to edit templates" is about writing. Read access needs no credentials, so browsing and running templates always works. Saving your edits back to GitHub does need a token, and until one is configured those controls are simply absent rather than shown broken. Your local edits still save to the working copy. Creating templates and connecting your GitHub account are done from Configure, not from the panel.
What does the Refresh button in the Templates panel do?
Refresh re-reads the catalog from GitHub — use it if a template you expect is not listed.
What happens if I load a catalog template over a working copy with unsaved edits?
Clicking a catalog entry loads it. Replacing a working copy that has unsaved edits asks first; replacing an untouched one is silent.
How are template steps displayed in the conversation?

Each step appears as its own node in the conversation, with a short title taken from its first heading and the full prompt available under a Task details disclosure. Each node shows its state on its left edge: Not run (muted), Running… (amber, pulsing), or Run (green) — so you can see at a glance how far through the recipe you are. Steps can also be edited, reordered and removed before you run them.
What does the run-next-step button do and when is it disabled?

The ▷| button runs the selected step and advances the selection to the next one, so repeated clicks walk the template one step at a time. This is the careful way through a template: you see each result and can correct course — or edit the next prompt — before continuing. The button is disabled when nothing is selected, and while a run-all is in flight.
What does the run-all-steps button do, and when should I use it?

The ▷▷ button runs every step from the current selection to the end, without stopping. Use it for a template you trust and have run before. For anything new, step through it once first — a template that goes wrong at step two will otherwise keep building on that mistake through step five.
How does the assistant behave while a template step is running?
While a step runs, the assistant works exactly as it would on a message you typed yourself — reading files, writing code, calling tools.
How do I run a shell command from the assistant message box?

The message box has two modes in one field: plain text is an instruction to the assistant, while a line starting with `!` is run as a shell command in your application's directory instead, with the output returned in the conversation. That is quicker than opening the Terminal for a one-off such as `!npm ls` or `!git log --oneline -5`. The placeholder says: "Message the agent or use the '!' to execute shell commands."
How should I write instructions to the Trustable assistant?

Name what you want changed and what the result should be, and say what to leave alone when it matters. The assistant can see your code, so you rarely need to describe it — but it cannot see your intentions, and standing intentions belong in `AGENTS.md` rather than in every message.
What can I see in the TruACP conversation area?

Every message — yours, the assistant's, tool output, template steps — appears there in order, and each block has a Copy action. It is also where you follow what the assistant actually did: which files it read, which it wrote, which tools it called. When a result surprises you, the answer is almost always visible in that transcript.
What is the preview panel in the workbench showing?

The right-hand pane runs your application live — what the assistant just built, a working React application with real navigation, not a mockup. Because it is the real application, you interact with it exactly as your users will: click through it, fill in forms, check the flows. That immediate feedback is the point of the two-pane layout — describe, watch, refine, without a build step in between.
How can I point the assistant at a specific element on the page instead of describing it?

The floating badge in the corner of the preview opens an element selector: Select picks one element on the page, Multiselect picks several. It solves the problem of describing where something is — rather than writing "the second heading inside the card on the right", you click the element itself and the assistant receives the reference, then you say what should change about it. For a change that touches several places, Multiselect gathers them into a single instruction.
